## One open line item, and a go-live date on the calendar

You're back in the same room as the last module — you, your Quality Analyst, your systems
administrator — but this time there's an agenda item with your name next to it: *eQMS
(electronic quality-management system) go/no-go*. Your Quality Analyst opens by handing you one
page, not twelve. It's her independent assessment, closed out: audit/logging, confirmed
implemented correctly, operating as intended, producing the desired outcomes. Physical and
environmental protection, same verdict. Account and identity management — the one she stopped
on — gets a single, specific line: *implemented and documented, but has not yet been exercised on
its first scheduled cycle.*

Your systems administrator jumps in before you ask. "I can run it this week. Takes maybe two
days once I actually sit down with it." That's a real offer, and it's tempting to just say "great,
run it, we'll talk Friday." But notice what that would actually be: postponing the decision, not
making it. The eQMS has a go-live date. Somebody has to decide, today, on the record, whether
Lakeshore operates it starting now with that one item still open, or holds the date until it
closes. Both are legitimate answers. "We'll figure it out informally and see how it goes" is not
one of them — and that's exactly the habit this whole course has been built to break.

This is the moment the last three modules were all pointing at. Categorize and Select decided
what the eQMS needed. Implement and Assess built it and checked it. Nobody yet has stood up and
said, out loud, with their name on it, "I've looked at what's left, and here's what Lakeshore is
doing about it." That's today's job, and it's yours — not your QA's, not your systems
administrator's.

## Why this step exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure Authorize and Monitor are built to prevent, and it's a different failure than
the one Implement and Assess guarded against. That pair stopped a team from believing an
unverified control. This pair stops a different, later problem: a verified gap that everyone
quietly tolerates because nobody wants to be the one who either blocks the go-live date or signs
their name to accepting the risk. Deficiencies don't usually get buried through malice. They get
buried because no single person was ever clearly the one whose job it was to decide, so the
decision never formally happens — it just sort of occurs, undocumented, by default, the day the
system goes live anyway because the date was already on the calendar.

You already know the ITSM (IT service management) shape of this problem, just under a different
name. Think about a release that reaches its go/no-go gate with one known, lower-severity defect
still open — not a blocker, but not nothing either. A mature release management practice doesn't
pretend the defect isn't there, and it doesn't automatically delay the release over it either. It
does something more specific: someone with the authority to make that call — a release manager,
a service owner, a change advisory board acting as a body — looks at the defect, decides whether
it's acceptable to ship with a documented workaround, logs it as a known error in the KEDB (known
error database) with an owner and a planned permanent fix, and the release proceeds on the record.
What never happens in a well-run practice is the defect quietly disappearing from the release
notes because raising it felt inconvenient the day before launch. **Authorize is that same gate,
aimed at a security and privacy risk decision instead of a software defect** — a named person,
reviewing a named gap, making an explicit, logged call instead of letting the go-live date make
the decision by default.

**Monitor** is the practice right after that gate that ITSM already trained you to expect:
**continual improvement**, applied specifically to the thing you just accepted. A known error
with a planned fix and no one ever checking back on it isn't really being managed — it's being
ignored politely. The same is true of a residual risk nobody revisits.

## The rule in plain English

**Authorize** means one accountable person — here, you, the Director — reviews what Assess
actually found (not what Select originally planned, not what Implement claims it built, but what
an independent check confirmed is true today) and makes an explicit, documented call: either the
eQMS's residual risk, as it stands right now, is acceptable to run on, or it isn't. If it's
acceptable, that acceptance gets named specifically — which gap, how long you're willing to carry
it, and what has to happen before you reconsider. A decision nobody can point to in writing isn't
an authorization. It's a shrug that happened to coincide with a launch date.

**Monitor** means that acceptance isn't the end of the conversation. It's a commitment to keep
checking — on a stated schedule, against stated triggers — whether the thing you accepted is
still acceptable, and whether anything else about the eQMS has changed since you made the call.

One thing to say plainly, and then not belabor, because this course has already said it at
length in the first three modules: **none of this is an actual federal "authorization to
operate."** Lakeshore is not a federal agency, and the eQMS is not a federal information system.
What you're about to do borrows the *ceremony* of that federal decision — one accountable person,
reviewing real evidence, on the record — not the legal instrument itself. Nothing below creates
any obligation to any federal authorizing body. It creates an obligation Lakeshore chose to carry,
to itself.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing — Authorize) | "...Chapter Two" | U.S. government work, public domain, safe to quote verbatim. States that Authorize means a determination that the risk is acceptable. | The decision you make today about the one open account-and-identity-management item. |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Appendix B (authorization to operate, sourced to OMB Circular A-130) | "Appendix B" | Same tier. Defines what an actual federal authorization to operate is and who issues one. | Quoted to show, precisely, what Lakeshore is *not* doing — and what it's borrowing the shape of instead. |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing — Monitor) | "...Chapter Two" | Same tier. States that Monitor means ongoing assessment, documenting change, reassessing risk, and reporting posture. | The standing eQMS monitoring plan this module builds. |

## The actual text

Authorize's one-line action, quoted verbatim from `sources/nist/sp-800-37r2-excerpt.md` (part of
the Figure 2 passage already quoted in full in `risk-frameworks-side-by-side` — this is the one
line this module actually acts on):

> Authorize the system or common controls based on a determination that the risk to
> organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation is
> acceptable.

Strip away "organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the
Nation" — language written for a federal agency, not Lakeshore — and what's left is the actual
mechanism: a determination. Not a feeling. Not a date arriving on a calendar. A determination,
made by someone, about whether a specific, known risk is acceptable.

Now the term this course has named but never actually quoted until this module. "Authorization to
operate" (ATO) is NIST's own glossary term, and the saved excerpt attributes its definition to a
separate source document NIST itself cites — OMB (the Office of Management and Budget) Circular
A-130 — not to SP 800-37 inventing the concept itself. Quoted verbatim:

> The official management decision given by a senior Federal official or officials to authorize
> operation of an information system and to explicitly accept the risk to agency operations
> (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), agency assets, individuals, other
> organizations, and the Nation based on the implementation of an agreed-upon set of security and
> privacy controls. Authorization also applies to common controls inherited by agency information
> systems.

Read that definition slowly, because every word of it is doing a job the eQMS decision also needs
done, with one critical substitution. "A senior Federal official" becomes you, the Director — not
because any law says so, the way it does for that federal official, but because Lakeshore needs
exactly one person whose name is on this decision, and that person has to be you. "Explicitly
accept the risk" is the operative phrase: not "the risk is probably fine," not "we'll keep an eye
on it" — explicit, on the record, naming the risk being accepted. "Based on the implementation of
an agreed-upon set of security and privacy controls" is exactly what Categorize, Select, Implement,
and Assess already gave you: a specific, documented, independently checked set of controls to
weigh the one open gap against.

Say it once more, plainly, and then move on: Lakeshore's eQMS decision is **not** this. No "senior
Federal official" exists here; no federal agency owns the eQMS; nothing about "the Nation" is at
stake. What you're borrowing is the shape of the decision — one accountable person, explicit
acceptance, on the record, tied to a documented control set — not the legal instrument the
definition above actually describes.

Monitor's one-line action, quoted verbatim from the same excerpt:

> Monitor the system and the associated controls on an ongoing basis to include assessing
> control effectiveness, documenting changes to the system and environment of operation,
> conducting risk assessments and impact analyses, and reporting the security and privacy
> posture of the system.

Four separate obligations live in that sentence: keep checking that controls still work, write
down what changes about the system or where it runs, keep reassessing risk rather than assuming
the original assessment ages gracefully, and report the system's standing to someone — not just
privately know it.

## The decision

Here's what actually happens in the room. You have one open item: the quarterly access-review
control, implemented and documented, not yet exercised on its first scheduled cycle. You have two
honest options, and both are defensible — which is exactly why this has to be a decision, not a
default.

**Option A: hold go-live** until the review actually runs. Clean, conservative, and not wrong.
Nothing about the eQMS absolutely requires launching today instead of in two weeks.

**Option B: authorize now, naming the gap as an accepted, time-bound residual risk, with a
remediation commitment attached.**

You take Option B, and here's the reasoning, said to your QA and your systems administrator in
the room, not just filed away afterward. The two control families Assess already confirmed —
audit/logging and physical/environmental protection — are both fully verified: implemented
correctly, operating as intended, producing the desired outcomes. The one open item isn't a
control that's missing or broken; it's a control that exists, is documented, and simply hasn't had
its first scheduled exercise yet. The exposure during that gap is real but bounded: a stale
account or a role mismatch that an on-time review would have caught, for however many weeks the
review is late. That's a risk worth naming and carrying briefly, not a reason to hold a three-site
go-live over a control that's already built and already scheduled.

So you say it, on the record, the way the ATO definition above describes: *"I'm authorizing the
eQMS for production use, effective today, across all three sites. I am explicitly accepting one
named residual risk: the first quarterly access review for account and identity management has
not yet run. I am not accepting this indefinitely. [Systems administrator], I need that first
review completed and its results reported to me within 30 days of today's decision — not
'sometime soon,' a specific window. If it finds nothing wrong, the acceptance closes clean. If it
finds something — a stale account, a mismatched role — we treat that as a new, immediate finding,
not something this authorization already waived."*

That sentence — a named gap, a named owner, a specific 30-day window, a stated consequence either
way — is what turns "I'll run it this week" into an actual authorization decision instead of an
informal promise. It's also, not incidentally, exactly what module 5 is going to need: a dated,
owned, specific remediation commitment is the raw material a POA&M (plan of action and milestones)
entry is built from. You haven't built that entry here — that's next module's job — but you've
just created the one thing it requires to exist.

## The ongoing monitoring plan

Authorize isn't a one-time stamp; it comes with a standing commitment to keep watching, per
Monitor's own four obligations above. Concretely, for the eQMS, that means:

- **The 30-day remediation check, specifically.** Did the first access review actually run? Did
  it find what it was designed to find, or did it turn up a stale account or mismatched role the
  system had been quietly carrying? Either answer gets reported back to you by name, not folded
  silently into next quarter's routine review.
- **The ongoing quarterly cycle, generally.** Once the first review clears, the same cadence
  continues on schedule — this module's accepted gap was about the *first* cycle specifically,
  not a reason to loosen the schedule going forward.
- **Audit/logging, spot-checked periodically**, not just confirmed once at Assess. A log that was
  capturing every CAPA (corrective and preventive action) and document-control change six weeks
  ago can silently stop doing so if a configuration changes; nobody should assume Assess's verdict
  ages forever.
- **A fresh look whenever something material changes about the eQMS** — a new site added, a new
  integration connected, a vendor patch applied, a new category of record stored in it. Any of
  those could change what Categorize originally concluded, which is exactly what Monitor's
  "documenting changes to the system and environment of operation" phrase is there to catch.
- **A standing trigger for revisiting this specific authorization**, not just a vague "we'll stay
  alert": if the overdue review turns up a real finding, if a control that cleared Assess ever
  stops operating as intended, or if the 30-day window passes with no review run at all, this
  authorization is reopened — it does not quietly keep standing on its own.

## The single sentence this course has been building toward

Here's why making this call is the same underlying decision as something you already understand
cold from a different vocabulary. In `csv-and-becs`, a validation package reaches its own go/no-go
moment: a Quality Validation Lead reviews the executed test evidence, including any open
deviations, and signs and dates an approval that the system may move to production — and from
that point forward, a periodic review keeps checking, on a schedule, whether the system is still
behaving the way that approval assumed. **Authorizing the eQMS today is that identical motion, one
layer removed from software validation and aimed at a security-and-access control instead of a
tested requirement: one accountable person looks at independently-verified evidence and a named
residual risk and says "acceptable, go live," and that decision comes bundled with an ongoing
commitment — Monitor here, periodic review there — to keep checking it stays true.** Different
vocabulary, different originating framework, same shape of decision, made by the same kind of
accountable person, for the same underlying reason: nothing proven once stays proven forever
without somebody committing to keep checking.

## What a reviewer would actually look for

What a competent reviewer — your CIO, an AABB assessor who happens to ask about the eQMS, or you
yourself revisiting this in six months — wants to find is a single document with your name on it,
dated the day of the decision, that names the specific gap, states explicitly that the risk is
accepted (not "noted" or "flagged" — accepted), and gives a specific remediation date. A bad
answer sounds like "we knew about the access review and just went live" with nothing written down
about who decided that was fine. A good answer produces exactly the sentence this module just
walked through, on paper, with a 30-day date on it.

## Common traps

**"We'll just keep an eye on it informally — no need to write anything down."** That's your
systems administrator's line from module 1, back again in a new disguise. An unwritten acceptance
isn't an authorization; it's the same ad hoc risk judgment this entire course exists to replace.
If the decision isn't written down with a name and a date, it didn't happen in any way that
survives a question six months from now.

**"Authorizing with an open item means the system isn't really secure yet."** No — it means the
risk was found, named, and deliberately accepted as acceptable for a bounded period, which is a
stronger position than a system that launched with the same gap nobody ever looked at closely
enough to name. An honest, time-bound acceptance is a sign the process worked. A system with zero
named residual risk at authorization is usually a sign nobody looked hard enough, not a sign
everything is actually perfect.

## What this means for your job

- **Never let a go-live date make the authorization decision by default.** If nobody explicitly
  said "I accept this risk," the launch happening anyway isn't an authorization — it's a decision
  that got made silently, by nobody, which is worse than either real option.
- **Demand a name, a specific gap, and a specific date before you sign anything.** "We'll monitor
  it" without a date attached isn't a remediation commitment; it's the same shrug this course keeps
  warning you about.
- **Treat Monitor as a real, standing obligation, not a one-time afterthought to Authorize.** A
  risk accepted and never revisited is functionally the same as a risk nobody ever named.
- **Ask what would make you revisit an authorization before anyone tells you to.** A new site, a
  new vendor patch, a control that stops working — if you can't name at least one concrete trigger,
  your monitoring plan is decorative.
- **When you explain this upward, to your CIO or sideways to an AABB assessor, say plainly that
  this is Lakeshore's own voluntary risk-acceptance discipline, not a federal requirement.**
  Overclaiming it as "our federal authorization process" the moment it sounds impressive is exactly
  the overstatement this course has warned against from its first module.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator asks, "Since we just authorized the eQMS using NIST's framework, did Lakeshore just issue a real federal authorization to operate?" What do you tell him?

No. An actual authorization to operate, per OMB Circular A-130's own definition that NIST's
document cites, is issued by a senior Federal official for a federal information system, and
explicitly accepts risk to agency operations and "the Nation." The eQMS is not a federal system,
and Lakeshore is not a federal agency — nothing about today's decision has any legal force outside
Lakeshore itself. What happened is that Lakeshore borrowed the *shape* of that decision — one
accountable person, explicit acceptance, documented evidence — entirely voluntarily, the same way
it already borrowed ICH Q9's structure and AABB's own accreditation structure elsewhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Why did the Director authorize the eQMS today instead of waiting the two days it would have taken to just run the overdue access review first?

Because the two confirmed control families (audit/logging, physical and environmental
protection) were fully verified, and the one open item was a control that exists and is
documented but simply hasn't had its first scheduled exercise — a bounded, well-understood gap,
not an unknown one. Waiting would have been defensible too; so would authorizing. What makes
authorizing now defensible, rather than reckless, is that it came with an explicit, named,
dated acceptance — not a quiet decision to just launch and hope the review happens eventually.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: If the 30-day access review turns up a stale account that should have been revoked weeks ago, does that mean the Director's authorization decision was wrong?

No — it means Monitor is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. The authorization didn't claim
the access list was clean; it explicitly named the fact that nobody had checked yet as the risk
being accepted, for a bounded window, with a commitment to look. Finding a real problem inside
that window is the monitoring plan working as designed, the same way module 3's assessment
finding the unrun review in the first place was the process working, not failing. What would
actually call the authorization into question is the 30-day date passing with still no review
run and nobody revisiting the decision.
:::

## Where this goes next

You've made and logged the eQMS's authorization decision — one named residual risk, accepted for
30 days, with a specific remediation commitment — and built the ongoing monitoring plan that
keeps checking it. That dated commitment is exactly what `poams-and-capas` needs to build a real
POA&M (plan of action and milestones) entry around, and to place next to a CAPA and show they're
doing the identical job in two different vocabularies.
